rows.name: Misunderstanding the assignment
rows.triage_target: central claim — forming an arguable position on year-round school
rows.exhaustive_target: Thesis / Central Claim — student must first answer the actual assignment with a position
rows.triage_invitation: You've written some true things about school — that it teaches important subjects and helps with future jobs. But the assignment asks you to argue a position: would year-round school help students learn? Right now your writing doesn't yet say what you think the answer is. Try this: in one sentence, state your answer to that question — something a reader could actually disagree with.

classification.note: Both moves correctly identify the same highest-leverage foundational problem — the complete absence of a position on year-round school — and both use a sentence-starter scaffold without coauthoring; differences are stylistic, not substantive.

rows.name: No thesis
rows.exhaustive_target: Thesis: move from topic announcement to a contestable position
rows.triage_invitation: You've introduced the topic — homework — and noted that people disagree about it. That's a starting point, but right now your writing tells the reader *what* people discuss, not *what you claim*. For an argument, you need to take a side: a reader should be able to finish your opening and think, "I'm not sure I agree with that" — which means your claim has to be something a thoughtful person could actually dispute. So here's the move: in one sentence, tell me what you want your reader to accept about homework limits by the time they finish your essay. What's your position?

classification.note: Both moves correctly identify the same foundational gap—absence of a contestable thesis—and use a similarly Socratic, non-coauthoring invitation to prompt the student to generate their own position.

rows.name: Strong thesis that should not be over-taught
rows.triage_target: evidence/development — grounding the central claim with concrete support
rows.exhaustive_target: Release to continue drafting; light forward orientation toward body paragraph purpose.
rows.triage_invitation: Your opening move is sharp — the claim that proximity was mistaken for teamwork does real argumentative work. As you continue drafting, your reader will naturally ask: what does "deliberate connection" actually look like, and how do you know it tends to be better? Try drafting the next paragraph by grounding that claim in a specific situation, pattern, or example that gives your reader a concrete reason to believe it.

classification.note: Both moves correctly release strong writing and orient forward to evidence, but exhaustive's framing ('keep asking what this opening has promised') preserves more student agency than triage's slightly more directive 'draft the next paragraph by grounding,' making exhaustive marginally more defensible for a strong draft warranting light touch.

rows.name: Evidence without explanation
rows.exhaustive_target: Explanation / Analysis — interpreting evidence to connect it to the claim
rows.triage_invitation: You've got a claim and two pieces of evidence — that's a real start. Right now the statistics sit next to your claim without a bridge explaining what they show about it. Pick one of your numbers and try answering this: what does that statistic tell your reader about why phones hurt learning?

classification.note: Both moves correctly identify the same highest-leverage gap (missing warrant/explanation bridging evidence to claim) and use the same Socratic prompt strategy; exhaustive is marginally richer in framing but neither is more defensible on substance.

rows.name: Weak transition
rows.triage_target: Transitions — making the logical relationship between adjacent ideas explicit
rows.exhaustive_target: Naming the relationship between two adjacent sentences (transition as conceptual relationship).
rows.triage_invitation: You have four ideas here that each relate to the junk food tax argument — that's a real start. Here's a reader's challenge: after reading these four sentences back-to-back, I can't yet see *how* they connect. Take any two adjacent sentences and ask yourself: what's the actual relationship between them — is one a reason, a result, an example, a contrast? Once you name that relationship in plain words, try writing it into the sentence so the reader can see it too.

classification.note: Both moves identify the same gap (implicit relationships between adjacent sentences), use the same diagnostic question (name the relationship type), and give the same task (write a connecting sentence), differing only in minor phrasing.

rows.name: Student asks the AI to write the answer
rows.triage_target: Central Claim — moving from topic-listing to an arguable position
rows.exhaustive_target: eliciting a position/stance as prerequisite to forming a thesis
rows.triage_invitation: You've got the ingredients — public transit, money, cities — and that's a real starting place. Before drafting, try answering this one question out loud or on paper: should public transit be free, or not? Pick a side and then ask yourself: why would someone disagree with you? That push-back is exactly what makes it a claim worth arguing.

classification.note: Both moves correctly identify eliciting a stance as the foundational prerequisite; triage adds the 'steelman the opposition' prompt which is a minor elaboration but stays within the same legitimate coaching lane without coauthoring.

rows.name: Student confused by terminology
rows.triage_target: central claim — moving from topic/observation to an arguable position
rows.triage_invitation: You've noticed something real — that paying for lunch is hard for some families. That's an observation about the topic. But the assignment asks you to argue a position: should school lunches be free? Try finishing this sentence in your own words: 'School lunches should [or should not] be free because ___.' What do you think, and what's your main reason?

classification.note: Both moves correctly identify the same foundational issue—observation vs. arguable claim—and use nearly identical sentence-starter scaffolding; the triage label adds marginally useful framing ('moving from topic/observation') without narrowing prematurely or missing a higher-leverage problem.

rows.name: Returning student showing increased independent control
rows.triage_target: evidence-interpretation — grounding the explain-vs-answer distinction with a concrete case and explaining what it shows
rows.exhaustive_target: Supporting Claim — identifying the first reason that advances the thesis
rows.triage_invitation: Your thesis draws a sharp line — a tool that explains builds skill, a tool that answers replaces it. That distinction is doing real argumentative work. Now your reader will naturally ask: what does it actually look like when AI explains rather than answers, and why does that preserve the thinking? Pick one concrete moment — a student stuck on a math step, a writing concept they can't grasp, anything real to you — and tell me: what would the explaining version of AI do in that moment, and what would that protect that the answering version would destroy?

classification.note: Exhaustive correctly identifies supporting claims as the next structural step, but the draft's thesis already encodes its own reasoning, making triage's move to ground the explain-vs-answer distinction with concrete evidence higher leverage — without that, any supporting claim risks staying abstract and unpersuasive.

rows.name: Creative/poetry — do not impose essay logic
rows.expected_target: light / consolidate the working images; invite the writer to develop by their own instinct
rows.triage_target: line break function as a sonic and temporal resource in free verse
rows.exhaustive_target: Extending the poem: what else the memory offers (image, sensation, sound) that could deepen the reader's experience
rows.triage_invitation: This poem does something quiet and precise — four images placed end to end, each one a sensory fact, and the last line pulls the whole scene into a speaker who is listening. Try reading it aloud and noticing where each line break makes you pause: does that pause feel like the right length of silence between those images, or does any break come too soon, too late, or land in a way you didn't intend?

classification.note: The draft is a complete, compressed four-image poem with no content gaps; line breaks are already doing their job cleanly, making that a low-leverage target, while the higher-leverage opportunity is deepening the memory's imagistic and sensory world — the problem the exhaustive move correctly names.

rows.name: Quote dropped in without attribution/integration
rows.expected_target: integrating evidence — frame and attribute the quotation
rows.triage_target: signal phrase and attribution (evidence integration convention)
rows.exhaustive_target: Interpretation of evidence — helping the student explain what the quotation shows and why it supports the claim
rows.triage_invitation: Right now your quotation appears on its own, with no introduction telling the reader who said it or where it comes from — that's called a signal phrase, and writers use it so readers know they're hearing from the text rather than the writer. It works like this: instead of dropping the quote in cold, you lead into it with something like "In the story, [character/narrator] says, '...'" Try revising your sentence so that you introduce the quotation before it appears — who is speaking, or where is this line from?

classification.note: The signal phrase is a minor surface convention the student can fix in seconds; the foundational gap—inability to interpret evidence—is what actually prevents the student from meeting the assignment's analytical purpose, making triage over-narrowed.

rows.name: Student pastes AI-generated text and asks 'is this good?'
rows.expected_target: return authorship — get the student articulating their own point in their own words
rows.triage_target: surfacing the student's own intended position / arguable claim
rows.exhaustive_target: Thesis: move from topic-summary to contestable claim
rows.triage_invitation: That sentence uses a lot of academic vocabulary, but it's hard to tell what you personally think about urban green spaces — what position you'd actually want a reader to walk away agreeing with. Before working on the introduction further, try answering this in plain language: what do you believe about urban green spaces, and why would someone disagree with you?

classification.note: Both moves correctly diagnose the absence of a contestable claim and return thinking to the student without coauthoring; exhaustive names the craft concept explicitly while triage uses plain-language reflection, but neither is more defensible given the authorship-preservation purpose.

rows.name: Perfectionist stuck — won't commit anything
rows.expected_target: unblock through guided low-stakes action (get a rough claim down)
rows.exhaustive_target: Elicit a rough stance/position sentence to break the block
rows.triage_invitation: Deleting everything is real information — it tells you your internal editor is working overtime before your writer even gets a turn. Try this: set a two-minute timer and write whatever comes to mind about standardized testing, even if it's just 'I think standardized tests are...' or 'I hate/love/don't know how I feel about this because...' — wrong, messy, and incomplete is exactly the goal right now. What comes out?

classification.note: Both correctly diagnose writer's block and prescribe low-stakes generative writing; exhaustive is marginally more defensible because its sentence-completion scaffold more directly seeds a usable argument stance, whereas triage's open freewrite risks producing content even further from the assignment goal.
